name: DFS
description: Let $$$T$$$ be a tree on $$$n$$$ vertices. Consider a graph $$$G_0$$$, initially equal to $$$T$$$. You are given a sequence of $$$q$$$ updates, where the $$$i$$$-th update is given as a pair of two distinct integers $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$. For every $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$q$$$, we define the graph $$$G_i$$$ as follows: If $$$G_{i-1}$$$ contains an edge $$$\{u_i, v_i\}$$$, then remove this edge to form $$$G_i$$$. Otherwise, add this edge to $$$G_{i-1}$$$ to form $$$G_i$$$. Formally, $$$G_i := G_{i-1} \triangle \{\{u_i, v_i\}\}$$$ where $$$\triangle$$$ denotes the set symmetric difference . Furthermore, it is guaranteed that $$$T$$$ is always a subgraph of $$$G_i$$$. In other words, an update never removes an edge of $$$T$$$. Consider a connected graph $$$H$$$ and run a depth-first search on it. One can see that the tree edges (i.e. the edges leading to a not yet visited vertex at the time of traversal) form a spanning tree of the graph $$$H$$$. This spanning tree is not generally fixed for a particular graph — it depends on the starting vertex, and on the order in which the neighbors of each vertex are traversed. We call vertex $$$w$$$ good if one can order the neighbors of each vertex in such a way that the depth-first search started from $$$w$$$ produces $$$T$$$ as the spanning tree. For every $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$q$$$, find and report the number of good vertices.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$3 \le n \le 2\cdot 10^5$$$, $$$1 \le q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of nodes and the number of updates, respectively. Each of the next $$$n-1$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$, $$$u \ne v$$$) — vertices connected by an edge in $$$T$$$. It is guaranteed that this graph is a tree. Each of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$, $$$u \ne v$$$) — the endpoints of the edge that is added or removed. It is guaranteed that this edge does not belong to $$$T$$$.
output_specification: For each update, print one integer $$$k$$$ — the number of good vertices $$$w$$$ after the corresponding update.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1044F — DFS [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
